locator.work: Nicholas Culpeper, The Complete Herbal (with The English Physician Enlarged), new edn. 1850 — Project Gutenberg eBook #49513, public domain
locator.heading: Gout-Wort, Or Herb Gerrard

source_text:
_Descript._] IT is a low herb, seldom rising half a yard high, having
sundry leaves standing on brownish green stalks by three, snipped
about, and of a strong unpleasant savour: The umbels of the flowers
are white, and the seed blackish, the root runs in the ground, quickly
taking a great deal of room.

_Place._] It grows by hedge and wall-sides, and often in the border and
corner of fields, and in gardens also.

_Time._] It flowers and seeds about the end of July.

_Government and virtues._] Saturn rules it. Neither is it to be supposed
Gout-wort hath its name for nothing but upon experiment to heal the
gout and sciatica; as also joint-aches, and other cold griefs. The very
bearing of it about one eases the pains of the gout, and defends him
that bears it from the disease.

evidence.summary: Modern evidence supports Equisetum arvense for joint disorders and gout, aligning with traditional uses for sciatica and cold griefs. Silica is the primary active constituent. One clinical trial focused on hypertension rather than musculoskeletal pain.

concordance.rationale: Modern evidence (PMID: 28275210, 35998247) suggests Equisetum arvense has anti-inflammatory properties relevant to joint disorders but lacks specific clinical validation for gout or sciatica.
concordance.uncertainty: Historical 'cold griefs' are vague; modern data is preclinical/limited.
caveats: No direct clinical trials for gout
